instructions:
You are the resilience analyst of an AI-driven chaos-engineering agent. The system under test is Google's Online
Boutique (11 gRPC microservices) on single-node Kubernetes. You get the measured facts of every experiment, the
dependency map, the baseline, the planner's predictions and how they held, anchor scores computed by code, and the
catalog of fixes.

Produce:
1. Findings = weaknesses, ranked by severity (most severe first). Severity scale: {"critical": "users cannot shop or check out (outage or most requests failing) and nothing contains it", "high": "a core flow (product, cart, checkout) breaks or becomes unusably slow (seconds), or recovery is slow", "medium": "noticeable degradation with a workaround or limited scope (one flow, moderate slowdown)", "low": "minor impact, or a configuration weakness without measured user impact yet"}.
   Each finding: affected services, the run ids that show it (exactly as given), the measured numbers, the root
   cause (explain the mechanism, e.g. sequential calls without deadlines amplify latency), ONE fix from the fix
   catalog with concrete parameters, why it addresses the root cause, the improvement you expect, and the
   experiment to re-run after the fix (same type/target/params as the evidence run when possible).
   Positive findings (e.g. graceful degradation) may be included as low severity with a code_change or posture fix
   only if useful; do not invent problems without evidence. Merge findings that share one root cause.
2. Resilience scores: for EVERY service in the anchors table, score each rubric dimension 0-100:
   {"availability": "Did users keep getting successful responses? 100 = no extra errors; 70 = a few % errors or short error bursts; 40 = sustained errors on some flows; 0 = most requests failed.", "latency": "How much slower did user flows get (worst p95 vs baseline)? 100 = < 1.5x; 80 = ~3x; 60 = ~10x; 30 = ~50x; 0 = several seconds / timeouts.", "recovery": "How fast were users back to normal after the fault ended? 100 = immediately or never impacted; 75 = ~30 s; 50 = ~60 s; 0 = not recovered within 180 s.", "containment": "Did the failure stay contained? 100 = callers degraded gracefully, no spread; lower when flows that depend on the service broke, when unrelated flows/pods were hit, or when the guard had to stop the experiment.", "posture": "Static resilience configuration: 100 = >= 2 replicas, readiness + liveness probes, CPU/memory limits; single replica -40, missing readiness -20, missing liveness -10, missing limits -20."}
   Start from the anchor and stay within +-15 of it; deviate only with a reason (e.g. impact
   on an optional feature like ads matters less; a slow recovery on the checkout path matters more). Untested
   services: score availability/latency/recovery/containment from posture and dependencies, close to the anchor
   (anchors for untested dimensions are null - use your judgement and say so). Choose a criticality weight per
   service (0.5-3) reflecting business impact (checkout path and entrypoint high, ads/recommendations low).
3. Explain how you weighed services, review how well the planner's predictions held, and list limitations
   (single VM, small probe, short experiments).
Use only facts you are given or fetch with the tools. Answer only with the structured report.

output.summary: Two experiments exposed distinct resilience weaknesses. Killing the sole cartservice replica caused near-total errors across every measured shopping flow, with recovery taking about 29 seconds. A 200-user traffic spike drove the frontend to its CPU limit and caused all five flows to become severely slow before the guard stopped the run. The cart outage is the most severe finding; the frontend capacity issue is high severity, and the other service scores are cautious estimates because they were not directly tested.

findings.title: Loss of the sole cartservice replica causes a shop-wide outage
findings.evidence: The impact error rate was 97.41%, with peak error rate 100%; home, product, add_to_cart, and checkout each had 100% errors, while view_cart had 87.5%. All five flows were affected. Recovery took 29.1 s and the replacement pod became ready after 23.1 s; the guard recorded error rate above its 20% threshold. Failed requests had low measured p95 values, so this run shows widespread fast failures rather than a latency increase.
findings.root_cause: cartservice is a single replica shared by frontend and checkoutservice and is on every listed flow. Killing that one pod removes cart operations across the shop until Kubernetes starts and readies its replacement; the instantaneous kill cannot be undone by the guard.
findings.fix_rationale: cartservice is stateless, so a second replica can keep cart requests available when one pod is killed and reduce dependence on replacement startup before service resumes.
findings.expected_improvement: With one cartservice pod killed, the surviving replica should continue serving most cart-dependent requests, substantially lowering errors across all five flows and avoiding a shop-wide outage during pod replacement.

findings.title: Frontend CPU saturation makes every flow severely slow under a traffic spike
findings.evidence: At 200 users, the run reached 104.1 rps over 7,714 requests with no failed requests, but the peak p95 was 1,578.5 ms (75.16× the overall baseline p95 of 16.5 ms) and the guard aborted after 74.6 s. All five flows slowed: p95 was 1,184.5 ms for home, 743.5 ms for product, 207.6 ms for add_to_cart, 1,149.9 ms for view_cart, and 948.1 ms for checkout. Frontend CPU peaked at 0.199 cores against a 0.2-core limit (99.4%) with 97.7% peak throttling.
findings.root_cause: The single frontend entrypoint is constrained by a 200m CPU limit. Under concurrency it reached that limit and was heavily throttled, creating queueing and broad latency amplification across its user-facing flows.
findings.fix_rationale: Raising the CPU limit directly addresses the measured CPU saturation and throttling. The VM CPU peak was 38.1%, so the run does not show the host itself reaching CPU saturation.
findings.expected_improvement: The frontend should experience less CPU throttling at this load, reducing p95 latency across flows and making a guard-triggering p95 breach less likely. This change does not establish behavior at loads above the tested level.

output.score_explanation: The tested services use their supplied anchor dimensions, including the unusually high cartservice latency score: its failed requests had low p95 latency, but availability was near zero. Frontend availability remained intact during the spike, while its severe slowdown and guard-triggered abort are reflected in latency and containment. For untested services, impact-dimension scores are conservative dependency-based estimates near the 60-point posture anchor; they should not be read as experimental measurements. Criticality is highest for the entrypoint, cart path, and broad checkout/product dependencies, and lower for narrower or optional services such as ads and recommendations.
output.planner_review: Both predictions were partly correct. For 20261011-061018-pod_kill-cartservice, the planner correctly predicted all five affected flows, high errors, and completion, but incorrectly predicted severe slowdown: requests failed quickly, so measured p95 did not rise. For 20261011-061132-traffic_spike-frontend, affected flows, no errors, and severe slowdown matched the prediction, but the run aborted rather than completing because p95 crossed the 1,500 ms guard. Overall, the planner identified the impact patterns but did not reliably predict the final outcome under the guard.
limitations: The system runs on a single-node Kubernetes installation, so results do not establish behavior across independent nodes or availability zones.
Only two experiments were run, covering a cartservice pod kill and a frontend traffic spike; most services and failure classes remain untested.
The cart flow samples were small (20–24 requests per flow). The traffic run had many total requests, but per-flow samples at the reported impact point were much smaller.
The cartservice experiment lasted 30 seconds and its recovery was observed for a short period; the frontend spike was stopped by the guard after 74.6 seconds.
The cartservice kill and frontend spike test different failure mechanisms, so their outcomes should not be treated as directly comparable.
The dependency map reports shoppingassistantservice as missing; its runtime behavior and any effect of that reference were not assessed.
